messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] None of the models pass GOF
messages.subject_clean: [distance-sampling] None of the models pass GOF
messages.body_plain:
Ana

You cover lots of topics in this email; hard to know where to begin.

It is unfortunate your data are spiked and doubly unfortunate that this was not diagnosed until the end of the three years of data collection.  Nevertheless, the purpose of binning is to get the detection into the correct "bin" if it was not in the correct "exact" distance because of rounding.  To get data into the correct bin, it seems the "preferred" distance (multiple of 5) should be in the centre of the bin, not at the edge; so I would use cutpoints different to the ones you have used.  I might also believe (but you know better because the data are yours) that rounding was less of a problem at small distances than at large distances--suggesting that you have narrower bins at small distances--there is no reason that the bins need to be of the same width: perhaps 0-1, 1-2, 2-3, 3-4, 4-6,...

Because you have binned the data, you do not have the Kolomogorov-Smirnov or Cramer von-Mises tests at your disposal and you must use the chi-square test (which is sensitive to the location of the cutpoints for binning).  The degrees of freedom of the chi-square test is u-q-1 where u is the number of bins (6 in the example you provide) and q is the number of parameters in your model.  If you fit a hazard rate model with 2 parameters and include site as a factor covariate (adding 2 more parameters to be estimated), I think you will end up with 6-4-1=1 degrees of freedom left for your test.  Should an adjustment term appear in the fitted model you will see the "no degrees of freedom for test" message.

If you are in this situation, then you are in the uncomfortable situation of making inference about thrush density based on a detection function model inconsistent with the data you observed.  You may say this lack of fit was caused by rounding of data in the field, but your inference will be somewhat tarnished.

I believe to get year-specific estimates you would need to include Region.Label in your model; give that a try.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] DSM and stratification by year
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cath, hi listfolk,

In some sense DSM is a post-stratification, but in the sense that you
are explicitly modelling how density changes as a function of the
covariates, rather than defining areas over which to estimate density.

To your questions:

1) the question here is do you think that detectability changes by year?
If so, it's appropriate. If you wanted to use year as part of the
spatial model (either via a GAM or GAMM) you'd be saying that
distribution changes per year. A simple smooth of year really just
changes the level of the density over the whole area for that year --
it's not going to change spatial distribution within the year. You would
need to look at more complex models for that.

2) When covariates are used in the detection function they are included
in the fitted spatial model as an offset or as a correction to the count
(see Miller et al, 2013). Once the model is fitted, they play no part in
the prediction (as we've dealt with detectability by that point). The
surface you produce is averaging over years.

Hope this helps!

cheers,
--dave

References

Miller, D.L., Burt, M.L., Rexstad, E.A. and Thomas, L. (2013) Spatial
models for distance sampling data: recent developments and future
directions (ed O Gimenez). Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 4, 1001–1010.

messages.body_plain:
Adrian

Correct that the Distance GUI can be made to 'fit' a flat detection function, whereas Distance in R cannot.  I presume you are trying to produce an abundance estimate, and in the situation where detectability is perfect, your abundance estimate is simply number seen scaled up by A/a (ratio of study area size to size of covered region), which you could code yourself.

The mildly tricky part is producing a measure of precision.  In the situation you describe, there would be no uncertainty in the parameters of the detection function (because there is no detection function), so you need only the encounter rate variance.  This can be computed using the varn() function inside the mrds package.

Pretend I have 20 strip transects, all of length 4 units, with detection out to truncation distance 1.  Size of covered region is then 160 units.  Suppose my study area is of size 1000 units (I cover 16% of the study area with my transects).  I fabricate the number of detections per transect as:
nvec=c(0,6,2,4,7,2,1,8,3,13,15,16,10,9,7,3,2,6,3,0)

such that there were 117 detections.  My abundance estimate is 117 * (1000/160) = 731.25

varn() can calculate the cv^2 of encounter rate  as:

> tmp <- mrds:::varn(lvec=rep(x = 4,times=20), nvec=c(0,6,2,4,7,2,1,8,3,13,15,16,10,9,7,3,2,6,3,0), type="R2")
> tmp
[1] 0.07180099

making variance of encounter rate

0.392

Variance of my abundance estimate is this encounter rate variance scaled by the A/a multiplier squared (delta method)

> (1000/160)^2 * 0.392
[1] 15.3125

Analytical normal-approximation CI would then be
> sum(nvec)*(1000/160) + c(-1, +1) * 1.96 * sqrt((1000/160)^2 * 15.3125)
[1] 683.3143 779.1857

Somebody on the list will set us right if I've messed up.

messages.body_plain:
Alejandra

Before discussing analysis, let me make a few comments about the design.  Your survey design is not the greatest.  Without replicate transects you will not be able to make inference to areas beyond the location you surveyed.  In addition, placing your survey effort parallel to the coast runs the risk of conflating changes in detectability (with increasing distance from transect) with a depth gradient that might influence distribution of dolphins.  It would have been preferable to have placed shorter transects perpendicular to the coast--this way you would have had replicate transects and detectability away from the transect would not have been confounded with potential changes in animal distribution associated with a depth gradient.  I also gather these were one-sided transects (observer looking only out one side of the aircraft--to sea); one-sided transects also create difficulties in determining whether animals close to the transects are included or excluded in your recording.  Challenging.

1--the size of the covered area is the truncation distance (perpendicular distance of farthest detection) times line length.
2--transects in different strata do not need to have equal line lengths
3--if you choose to analyse these data, you would use conventional distance sampling, but you would fit a number of models to the data to determine which model is preferable for the data.

Consult the literature and lecture material available at our website http://distancesampling.org/whatisds.html to get a better perspective on the fundamentals of distance sampling.

messages.body_plain:
Rafael

Aggregation of animals does not violate any distance sampling
assumptions; no distribution of animals across the study area is assumed
by distance sampling.  The design assumption of distance sampling
(Buckland et al 2015 Section 1.7) is that animals are distributed
uniformly at all distances from the line *out to the truncation
distance* for lines and distributed according to a triangular
distribution for points.

However line transect distance sampling was intended for use with
populations that are sparsely distributed.  With the concentration at
roost sites, an observer will struggle to record distances to many many
individuals.  It might be the case that a hybrid stratified approach,
using perhaps photos to count animals in high density strata such as
roost sites and possibly point transects in a medium density stratum in
city parklands.  There might be a low-density stratum in built-up areas
of the city where birds are unlikely to be located. However, care will
need to be take to ensure the triangular distribution of birds at points.

messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] transect length and encounter rate
messages.body_plain:
Hi Derek,

Regarding your first question, I don't think you can change transect length to obtain a minimal encounter rate variance. The encounter rate variance (which represents the variance in number of detections as a function of units of effort) is a function of the degree of clustering of the animal population you are trying to survey, so it is not something that you can control. Having said that, placing transects perpendicular to gradients of density will help, because you will tend to make counts more similar across transects.
Regarding the second, there is absolutely no problem in having many transects without observations. For the same amount of total effort, the larger the number of transects the better, for at least 3 reasons: (1) better spatial coverage; (2) better estimates of encounter rate variance and (3) the more likely it is that the underlying assumptions about animal distribution within the covered strips are valid (uniform in lines and triangular for points, which is ensured by design given the random placement of transects in the study area). Of course that might come at a logistic cost, but that is a cost to weight against the above mentioned benefits.
Hope this helps,
Tiago

Hi Derek,

You have a problem, because your situation was not what I was expecting. My suggestions were from a survey design point of view, before data collection. I am NOT suggesting  "segmenting it randomly and analysing it as many short transects", in fact I advise you against that procedure.

If you only have one transect of 40 km, you can't simply cut it into 1000 transects of 40 meters and off you go. That is akin to pseudoreplication, because you treat each segment as an independent sampling unit, when they are not. The consequences are:
1. The point estimates will remain exactly the same one way or the other
2. The variance will be artificially decreased as you increase the number of transects - that you can change your variance estimates depending on an arbitrary choice of segment number/lengths should tell you there's something not adequate about it.

So, all in all, you do not have many transects, you have just one, and there's no analysis that will get you out of that. At best you might obtain the variance based on assumptions (see the Distance manual for possible options, including a Poisson or overdispersed Poisson assumption), but that has it's downsides.

Further, after considering that, if you have transects along roads you might have a problem, because the underlying assumption that transects have been placed at random with respect to the animals is violated, and if the animals do respond to roads, you could considerably underestimate or overestimate density.

Sorry for the promotion of my own work, but take a look at this paper for why that is the case and a possible solution (if you happen to have information about the distribution of animals with respect to the road from an independent source):

Marques, T. A.; Buckland, S. T.; Bispo, R. & Howland, B. 2013 Accounting for animal density gradients using independent information in distance sampling surveys Statistical Methods and Applications 22: 67-80

Best

T

When I use the parameter estimate from the half-normal model with no adjustments as the starting value when fitting the model with one adjustment term, my results match those in the example. messages.body_plain:
Hi Derek, Pierre, list

In my opinion, and road issues aside, provided that the one transect covers adequately the entire area one wants to make inferences for, then having a single transect with say 100 km, that one subdivides into 100 1 km segments, and then analyses every other one (so 50 transects), is not breaking any "statistical" rules. Probably someone will add to the discussion and tell me otherwise.

Now this is not me recommending that process, because the truth is that this is only reasonable if the coverage of the survey area is adequate, where adequate here is a vague concept, and you are much better off starting with a sensible survey design for making the inferences that you are interested in making. Also, it seems ineffective for logistical reasons, as you are having to travel across all the off effort areas.

Coming down to Pierre's point, I believe even the correlation that is induced because the segments were originally along "the same transect" is, to some extent, not an issue. Just in the same way as if one placed a design like the one below with just the blue lines considered on effort and the orange lines off effort, each transect would be considered an independent sampling unit, independently of them being along several different transects originally - we know that spatial autocorrelation will be present to a larger or smaller degree depending on the "clumpiness" of the population, but in conventional distance sampling we simply treat the transects as independent sampling units (that is e.g. why under a bootstrap it is recommended that you bootstrap lines, not detections).

See the study area below as an example, where effectively a single transect was conducted. You could obtain a density estimate from the blue lines as (much smaller) transects, and a robust variance around it. But then...by the same token, you could get one from the orange transects. How would you then combine the two? You can imagine this example being extended to having many subsets of transects. Depending on having or not to pool data for the detection function across subsets, these might correspond to independent or correlated density estimates, and hence how one would combine these to obtain the density estimate of interest might not be straightforward.

To conclude, my final advice is, perhaps not surprisingly... ignore all the above as it's possibly just causing confusion and opening a can of worms. Also because if you do have the entire area of inference covered, then the variance estimates from usual Distance sampling estimators are less than ideal, since they assume that you are covering a subset of a larger region such that finite correction factors are not used. But I felt I had to answer given Pierre's prompt. So: Plan your survey to have many lines, perpendicular to potential existing density gradients for the species of interest.

cheers,

T

PS -
As an aside, if anyone out there actually has:
1. a single transect
2. covering the entire survey area they want to make inferences for
3. ideally not from roads or any other linear structure potentially promoting a density gradient)
please contact me off the list. I'd like, (time permitting!) to explore some ideas under that setting.

To echo some of Tiago's sentiments:

There will be plenty of challenges to any biological survey: poor weather, equipment malfunction, tiring work, difficult measurements.  There will be no shortage of actors that will conspire to foil your intention of making defensible inferences about the population you are studying.  These difficulties will arise regardless of whether the survey design is good or poor.  Design is a feature of the survey over which the investigator has the greatest control.

A sensible approach is to *start* with a competent survey design.  If the design is poor, these other events outside investigator control cannot improve the inferences drawn.

messages.body_plain:
Ana Maria

It is not possible to answer all of your questions from the information you provided.  But here are a few observations:

- the MCDS engine is the multiple covariate distance sampling engine, permitting the use of covariates in modelling the detection function.  You do not mention what covariates you have included and whether you have allowed adjustment terms to be included along with covariates.  It is common for problems such as yours to arise when adjustment terms are combined with covariates.  Remember, the principle of parsimony is to use the simplest model that provides an adequate explanation to the data.  Ask a) do you need covariates; b) if you need covariates do you also need adjustments.  I suspect the answer to a) is perhaps no and b) almost certainly no.

- I would also not recommend basing the estimate of encounter rate variance upon an *assumption* of Poisson distribution of animals.  This should only be used if there are too few replicate transects to produce an estimation of encounter rate variability from the survey data.

- if you want a detection function that is the same across strata (assuming there is justification for this) and stratum-specific abundance estimates, you would select this arrangement of levels of resolution for estimation of various quantities

Further to Eric's response, if you are using covariates in addition to distance
in the detection function, and these covariates are different in different
strata (or are at the sample or observation level), then it makes sense to fit a
global detection function but predict detection probability by stratum, so that
Distance can account for the fact that differences in covariates between strata
will cause differences in detectability between strata.

To do this, in the Estimate tab, under "Quantities to estimate and level of
resolution", in the detection function line, you tick both the Global and
Stratum boxes.  (This means estimate a global function, predict by stratum --
for more info see the online help.)

Pierre

It is not a simple calculation to determine CV as a function of sample size for distance sampling.  It depends upon additional factors, such as the variability in number of detections between survey points.

This paper by Prof Buckland describes a detailed songbird study he conducted and provides a comparison of the relative number of hours of effort necessary to achieve desired levels of precision (CV) for different species in his field study.  Perhaps that study may be of use to you.
